# SK2130 — A static field initializer reads a field declared below it

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A static field's initializer reads another static field of the same type that is declared after it, and field initializers run in declaration order, so the read sees `default` rather than the initialized value.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `StaticMemberInitializerReferesToMemberBelow` (`resharper_static_member_initializer_referes_to_member_below_highlighting`) |

## Why

Static field initializers are emitted into the static constructor in the order the fields are written down. An initializer that names a field below it therefore runs before that field has been given its value, and reads zero, or null. Nothing throws, nothing warns, and the value is wrong for the life of the process — the field is simply never right, so there is no first failure to bisect to. ⚠ **Three neighbouring shapes look identical and are all correct, which is why the rule is exact about the construct rather than about the direction of the reference.** A static *property* is a method that runs when it is called, so a getter naming a field below it reads whatever that field holds at that moment. A static *method* is ordered against nothing. And a **static constructor runs after every field initializer**, so a read from there sees a fully initialized type. Only a field initializer is ordered against other field initializers.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static class Defaults {
    public static readonly string Path = Root + "/cache"; // Root is still null here
    public static readonly string Root = "/var/lib";
}
```

Write:

```csharp
static class Defaults {
    public static readonly string Root = "/var/lib";
    public static readonly string Path = Root + "/cache";
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The referenced field must carry an initializer of its own**, and that requirement is about the message being true rather than about the count. A field with no initializer reads as `default` from an earlier initializer *and* from a later one, so the declaration order is not what makes it default and a finding blaming the order would point at the wrong thing; the same holds for a field the static constructor assigns, because the static constructor runs after every initializer regardless of where the field is written down. ⚠ **A `const` is excluded on both sides**: its value is substituted at compile time, so no ordering between two of them exists. ⚠ **A read inside a lambda, an anonymous method or a local function is excluded**, and this is the exclusion that would otherwise make the rule wrong on idiomatic code — `static Func<int> f = () => later;` stores a delegate whose body runs when somebody invokes it, long after every initializer has finished, and deferring the read is the ordinary way to *repair* this defect. `nameof(Later)` reads nothing and is excluded. ⚠ **Only within one file.** A `partial` type's parts have no stated initializer order between them; it follows the order the files reach the compiler, which is a build detail rather than something the source says. That is the case ReSharper's own description calls the worst one, and declining it is the honest answer, because a cross-file finding would not be reproducible from the file it lands in — which is exactly what `scope: Semantic` promises the analysis cache. A read of another type's static field is excluded: that type's initializers run on first access, not in this type's order. Report-only, because the repair is to move a declaration and which of the two moves is right depends on what else in the type depends on the order. Generated code is excluded.
